The Group of 77 and China renews its unwavering commitment to multilateralism, international cooperation, and the purposes and principles of the United Nations. The group pledges to continue to advance its three interlinked pillars, peace and security, human rights, and development, in a balanced manner, and calls on all member states to renew the multilateral spirit that gave birth to the organization for the benefit of present and future generations. The group also emphasizes that we must join hands to realize the 2030 agenda, leaving no country and no person behind, and building together a just, inclusive, and better world, respecting, promoting, and protecting human rights for all. The group also reaffirms that the Commission for Social Development has the primary responsibilities for the follow-up to the Copenhagen Declaration and Programme of Action, and stresses its role in contributing to the follow-up to the 2030 agenda. The Group of 77 and China reaffirms that all humans are equal in dignity and rights, as recognized in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action. The group also stresses that all human rights are universal, indivisible, and interdependent and interrelated, and the international community must treat them, human rights, globally in a fair and equal manner, on the same footing and with the same emphasis. Mr. Chair, the group would like to remind delegations that is the traditional proponent of four draft resolutions reflecting our shared priorities and collective commitments, meaning implementation of the outcome of the World Summit for Social Development and of the 24th Special Session of the General Assembly, follow-up to the 13th anniversary of the International Year of the Family and Future Needs, follow-up to the Second World Assembly on Aging, Global call for concrete action for the total elimination of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia, and related intolerance, and for the comprehensive implementation of and follow-up to the Durban Declaration and Program of Action. Thirty years after the World Summit for Social Development, we acknowledge the progress made in advancing the core pillars of Copenhagen Declaration. Yet, we remain deeply concerned that poverty, inequality, exclusion, and challenges to achieving full and productive employment and decent work for all persist, compounded by new and emerging global challenges. In that regard, we welcome the hosting by the State of Qatar of the Second World Summit for Social Development, held from 4 to 6 November 2025, which reaffirmed the commitment to the Copenhagen Declaration and its Programme of Action on Social Development and to its implementation, while providing renewed momentum towards the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The group also underscores the need to strengthen inclusive social policies and programs, including family-oriented policies and programs through concrete strategies that build national capacities within a comprehensive approach to development as catalyst for reducing poverty and hunger, promoting the well-being of all at all ages, supporting children's development, and breaking the intergenerational cycle of poverty. At the same time, as the global population ages, we must also foster an enabling environment for the equal and meaningful participation of older persons by combating discrimination and safeguarding their rights and dignity. The Group of 77 and China reaffirms its strong opposition to all forms of discrimination, including racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance. and expresses concern at the alarming rise in religious hatred and intolerance. The group calls upon member states and the international community to condemn religious intolerance and hatred, foster dialogue, tolerance, and respect for cultural, ethnic, and religious diversity. The legacy of colonialism, slavery, and systemic exploitation has created deep-rooted global inequalities that persist across generations. Advancing reparatory justice is vital in addressing global inequality through structural reforms in global governance, trade, debt, finance to advance the SDGs. Mr. Chair, the Group of 77 and China recommit to eliminating all forms of discrimination, violence against all women and girls. and to ensuring their empowerment in all spheres of life, since achieving gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls, as well as the full, equal, and meaningful participation of women, are also indispensable to just and inclusive societies. The G77 and China also stresses the importance of redoubling efforts to ensure full and equal access to education, employment, and healthcare for persons with disabilities, and of strengthening support for youth, through inclusive education, training, skills development, addressing digital literacy challenges, and promoting employment. The Group of 77 and China reaffirmed it is crucial to cooperate internationally to ensure safe, orderly, and regular migration, involving full respect for human rights and the humane treatment of migrants, regardless of their migration status, refugees, and displaced persons. The Group also stresses that migrants positively contribute to sustainable development, while recognizing that the roles and responsibilities of the countries of origin, transit and destination should be appropriately balanced. The group further commits to combat misinformation and disinformation, negative stereotyping, and misleading narratives that generate negative perceptions of migration and migrants. In conclusion, the Group of 77 and China remains firmly committed to the promotion and protection of human rights and to advancing social development. We wish this session of the Third Committee every success and look forward to counting on the constructive participation of all delegations in the consultations on the resolutions that the group will be introducing during this session. Mr. Chair, I wish to congratulate you on the assumption of the chairmanship of this committee and wish you all the best. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the member states of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation under agenda item 71 on the promotion and protection of human rights. The OIC group reaffirms that all human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent, and interrelated, and must be treated fairly and equally. Their promotion and protection should be pursued through constructive dialogue and international cooperation in accordance with the principles of impartiality, objectivity, and non-selectivity, while taking into account national and regional particularities and different historical, cultural, and religious backgrounds. The group stresses the importance of ensuring equal attention to civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights including the right to development, and of protecting the rights of women, children, youth, older persons and persons with disabilities, as well as protecting and empowering the family in accordance with relevant OIC resolutions. The Group wishes to highlight three pressing concerns. High among the Group's priorities is the plight of the Palestinian people under Israel's illegal occupation. Despite the universal rights guaranteed by the UN Charter and international human rights instruments, the Palestinian people remain deprived of their rights, foremost among them their inalienable right to self-determination. The OIC Group strongly condemns the Israeli aggression against the Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip and the continuing violations across the occupied Palestinian territory. which have killed and injured tens of thousands of Palestinians, devastated civilian infrastructure, and deprived civilians of their basic human rights. The group categorically rejects any attempt to forcibly displace Palestinians from their homeland. Israel, the occupying power, must comply with international law, including the Fourth Geneva Convention, fully respect the ceasefire, protect civilians, and ensure safe, sustained, and unhindered humanitarian access throughout Gaza. We condemn all attacks and illegal measures against UNRWA and call for adequate and sustained political, legal, and financial support for the agency. The group further condemns Israel's illegal policies and practices in occupied West Bank, including East Al-Quds, notably settlement expansion, land confiscation, settler terrorism, forced displacement, and attempts at annexation. These measures are null and void under international law, undermine the Palestinian people's right to self-determination, and destroy the prospects of the two-state solution. The group rejects any attempt to fragment the occupied Palestinian territory or separate Gaza from the West Bank. including East Al-Quds, and reaffirms its support for an independent and sovereign state of Palestine on the borders of 4th June 1967, with East Al-Quds as its capital. The group reaffirms that Israel has no sovereignty over East Al-Quds or its Islamic and Christian holy sites. We condemn the repeated incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque, Al-Haram Al-Sharif, restrictions imposed on Palestinian worshippers, and attempts to alter the existing historical legal status quo or the character of the city. We stress that the entire area of Al-Aqsa Mosque, Al-Haram al-Sharif, is a place of worship exclusively for Muslims. Mr. Chair, the dehumanization of the Palestinian people and statements inciting hatred, violence, and genocide are closely linked to the group's second pressing concern. The group is gravely concerned by manifestations of intolerance, discrimination, hate speech, incitement and violence based on religion or belief, including the burning of the Holy Quran. Such acts violate the religious and cultural rights of Muslims and cannot be justified under the pretext of freedom of expression. which entails duties and responsibilities. The OIC group welcomes the adoption without a vote of General Assembly Resolution 80/200 on combating intolerance and violence based on religion or belief. We also reaffirm the importance of fully implementing General Assembly Resolution 79/316 on promoting interreligious and intercultural dialogue and tolerance in countering hate speech. These resolutions provide an important framework for combating religious intolerance and protecting persons, religious symbols, holy books, and places of worship. We call upon all States to implement them fully and adopt appropriate legal measures to prevent such acts and ensure accountability. The Group stresses the urgent need to combat Islamophobia, which threatens peaceful coexistence and social cohesion. We welcome the appointment of the United Nations Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia and reaffirm our commitment to working closely with him. Mr. Chair, the third pressing concern is the continued plight of Rohingya Muslims and other minorities in Myanmar. The group strongly condemns the atrocities perpetrated against the Rohingya and calls for urgent action to uphold their rights, end their targeting and stigmatization, address the root causes of the crisis, and create the conditions necessary for the safe, voluntary, dignified, and sustainable return of all displaced Rohingya, including those who have sought refuge in Bangladesh. The group commends Bangladesh and other OIC member states for hosting Rohingya refugees and calls upon the international community to provide adequate and sustained support. We further urge continued support for international efforts to ensure justice and accountability for the Rohingya people. In conclusion, the OIC group reaffirms its commitment to promoting and protecting all human rights in accordance with international law, guided by equality, justice, tolerance and mutual respect. We will continue to work with all partners to foster dialogue and understanding among cultures and civilizations, and ensure that no people or community is left behind in the enjoyment of human rights and fundamental freedoms. I thank you, Mr. Chair.

I have the honour to deliver a joint statement on behalf of a cross-regional group of 28 member states, namely Antigua and Barbuda, Belarus, Plurinational State of Bolivia, Burkina Faso, Cambodia, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Cuba, Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Islamic Republic of Iran, Lao People's Democratic Republic, Mali, Nicaragua, Niger, Pakistan, Russian Federation, South Sudan, Sri Lanka, State of Palestine, Sudan, Uganda, Bolivian Republic of Venezuela, Zimbabwe, and my own country, China. Today's world is plagued by rampant unilateralism and the raging unilateral coercive measures. History has proven that the UCMs are a major source of international turbulence and disorder. As the United Nations enters its ninth decade, the international community must remain clear-headed, strengthen unity and cooperation, and firmly oppose and bring an end to such unlawful practices. Developing countries and their peoples continue to bear the brunt of UCMs, which violate the principle of sovereign equality and cooperation. interfere in other countries' internal affairs, run counter to the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations, and undermine the foundation of multilateralism and international rule of law. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development underscores the equal enjoyment by all states of the development dividends, and strongly urges states to refrain from promulgating and applying any unilateral economic, financial or trade measures not in accordance with international law and the Charter of the United Nations. Regrettably, despite repeated calls by the international community for the urgent lifting of UCMs, These unlawful measures continue to have devastating, sometimes even life-threatening consequences for countries and their peoples. UCMs compounded by secondary sanctions and overcompliance exacerbate existing humanitarian and economic challenges and threaten food, energy, and financial security. The growing use of tariffs as a tool of unilateral coercion, including additional tariffs based on unilateral determinations under domestic law and imposed under the pretext of national security or human rights, further politicizes economic and trade issues, undermines the multilateral trading system, disrupts global industrial and supply chains, and impede the efforts of countries concerned to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. Moreover, UCMs severely violate the basic human rights, including the right to life, health, development, and education, and impede the ability of targeted countries to realize those rights. The Special Rapporteur on the negative impact of UCMs on the enjoyment of human rights for the UN Human Rights Council pointed out unilateral sanctions have led to shortages of healthcare services, medication, and energy supplies in sanctioned countries, with persons in vulnerable situations such as women, children, and the elderly facing particularly dire circumstances. We are also concerned that unilateral coercive measures and overcompliance have limited the ability of affected countries to access and acquire foreign investments and technology and hindered international cooperation in culture, arts, sports, travel, people-to-people exchanges, and transports, including civil aviation. Chair, we welcome the 2026 ministerial declaration of the Group of 77 and China on reaffirming that the imposition of coercive economic measures, including unilateral sanctions against developing countries, does not contribute to economic and social development, including dialogue and understanding among countries. We highlight the Non-Aligned Movement's declarations and communicates on condemning the promulgation and application of unilateral coercive measures, including those measures used as tools for political, economic, financial pressure against any country, in particular the developing countries. We recognize the work done by the Special Rapporteur on the negative impact of UCMs on the enjoyment of human rights for the UN Human Rights Council and take note of the reports, country visits and statements delivered by the Special Rapporteur. We reaffirm our opposition to unilateral coercive measures and call on the few Western countries to heed the just cause of the international community honour their commitments to upholding the UN Charter and international law, and immediately, unconditionally, and completely lift all UCMs. We also call upon Member States, the UN system, and other international organisations to jointly oppose such unlawful practices and help targeted countries mitigate their plight. We also request the Secretary-General to continue monitoring the imposition of unilateral economic measures as a means of political and economic coercion. The current circumstance calls for solidarity and unity, rather than confrontation and division, to address global challenges and promote and protect human rights for all. Thank you, Chair.

It may seem tempting to believe that in times like these, human rights are somehow less important than peace, security, or development, that they are a luxury to be pursued only once certain level of stability or prosperity has been achieved. Nothing could be further from the truth. Respect for human rights is not the sole preserve of peaceful and prosperous societies. Rather, it is an essential condition for building them. Europe's own history has taught us this lesson at enormous cost. Our continent has known war, authoritarianism, and grave violations of human rights. We do not claim to have overcome all our challenges. But our experience has shown us that reconciliation, lasting peace and sustainable development require respect for human rights, the rule of law, democracy and institutions strong enough to protect them. It is therefore precisely the wrong time to allow the weakening of the international human rights system painstakingly built over decades. It's time to defend it and make it work better. Chair, the Third Committee has an important role in this regard. The EU will engage actively across all agenda items of this committee. Protection of human rights, gender equality, social development, fighting racism, crime prevention and criminal justice all go hand in hand to achieve the same shared goal, a better life for all. Our commitment is to all human rights, civil, political, economic, social and cultural. And this includes the right to development as reflected in the 1986 declaration. The EU continues to translate this commitment into practice through our leading political and financial support for the SDGs and the 2030 Agenda. Our own history has taught us that there can be no lasting peace without justice and accountability. We therefore reaffirm our unwavering support for the international criminal justice system, particularly the International Criminal Court, and reject attempts to undermine its independence and integrity. The core message of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is clear. All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. And we will continue to combat all forms of discrimination, hatred and violence, whether based on the color of your skin, how you worship, who you love or who you are. The EU remains firmly committed to advancing gender equality, the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by all women and girls. and their empowerment in line with the global commitments we have all made. Equality in law is not enough. We need to take a transformative approach to actively address and dismantle the structural barriers and underlying root causes of gender inequalities and take proactive measures to achieve substantive equality for all. Equal rights, opportunities and dignity for women and girls benefit our societies as a whole, and this is what the gender equality agenda is about. It is an agenda that unites us, and we will continue to defend this unity and reject forces that try to divide and polarize us. We also must defend a safe and enabling space for civil society. We may not always agree with what civil society, journalists, or human rights defenders have to say about our governments and our policies, but open debate, peaceful dissent, and scrutiny are not threats to democratic societies, they help them thrive. And we must ensure that digital technologies, including AI, are developed and used in ways that are human-centric and never undermine human rights and fundamental freedoms. Chair, inevitably, our deliberation will be impacted by the challenges and horrors of the world around us, and it's our responsibility to address those. For more than four years, Russia has continued its war of aggression against Ukraine, in blatant violation of international law, including the UN Charter. The human cost continues to grow. UN human rights monitors have documented rising, systematic, and deliberate Russian attacks on Ukraine's civilian, cultural, and energy infrastructure, alongside widespread and systemic torture, ill treatment, and summary executions of Ukrainian civilian detainees, and unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children. We condemn in the strongest possible terms these atrocities. Russia and its leadership must be held accountable. We have become accustomed to Russia using this Committee to try to justify its aggression and to downplay its catastrophic impact. We ask other delegations to reject this politicisation of our work. The EU condemns the structural system of human rights violations in Russia, which are part of a further intensifying systematic, state-sponsored internal repression. We condemn all violations of international law in the occupied Palestinian territory and remain gravely concerned by the devastating humanitarian crisis in Gaza. We urge Israel to abide by its obligations under international law and immediately remove all restrictions to access and allow sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance throughout Gaza. We call for the permanent disarmament of Hamas and other non-state armed groups and the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Gaza Strip. Hamas cannot be part of any solution in Gaza. We regret the lack of progress in the implementation of the ceasefire and all other provisions of UN Security Council Resolution 2803, and reiterate our call on all actors to implement them. We condemn the continued and growing settler violence in the West Bank and Israel's unilateral actions aimed to expand its presence in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, which undermine the prospects for a two-state solution. We remain deeply concerned by deteriorating human rights situations in many countries around the world, whether driven by war and armed conflict, democratic backsliding, or growing authoritarian tendencies. In this regard, we refer to the recent EU statement under item 4 of the Human Rights Council. Chair, in this session, the EU will present the following resolutions: First, on the human rights situation of Rohingya Muslims and other minorities in Myanmar, together with the OIC. Nine years after the military operations that led to the mass exodus of Rohingya, and more than five years after the military coup, The Rohingya and the people of Myanmar have suffered too much and far too long. We must continue to shine a spotlight on this unacceptable situation. Second, we will also present the resolution on the human rights situation in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. The systematic, widespread, and gross human rights violations in one of the world's most closed societies require sustained international attention. All EU Member States are also members of the Interregional Task Force presenting the biennial resolution on a moratorium on the use of the death penalty. This remains an important priority. Reported executions rose sharply in 2025, driven largely by a small number of countries. Yet, the broader global direction remains clear. Some 170 countries have now abolished or introduced a moratorium on the death penalty, either in law or in practice. That's remarkable progress since the General Assembly adopted its first moratorium resolution in 2007. Chair, defending the human rights system also means being willing to reform it. The UN faces a severe liquidity crisis. Through the UN80 initiative, we are collectively considering how this organization can become more efficient, effective, and focused on delivering results. The EU strongly supports these efforts. However, reform must strengthen and not weaken the human rights pillar. It must safeguard the integrity, independence, normative role and operational capacity of the UN human rights architecture, including through adequate, predictable and sustainable funding. And in the Third Committee, the EU is ready to do its part. Almost all resolutions presented by the EU and its Member States in this Committee are already biennial or triennial, and we are ready to consider further steps. However, reform and efficiency efforts must be a shared responsibility, undertaken collectively and on a balanced and equitable basis. We encourage you, Chair, and the Bureau to play an active role in helping all delegations deliver on this shared commitment so that we can devote more time to what matters most: implementation and impact of our resolutions on people's lives. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of the European Union, and I now give the floor to the distinguished permanent representative of Jamaica, speaking on behalf of CARICOM, to be followed by Cuba. Jamaica, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. I do have the honor of delivering this statement on behalf of the 14 member states of the Caribbean Community. We congratulate you and the members of the Bureau on your election to guide this committee's work. during the 81st session and assure you of CARICOM's full support. CARICOM aligns with the statement delivered by Uruguay on behalf of G77 and China. And we thank the Secretary General and the relevant UN agencies for the reports provided under the respective agenda items, which will guide our discussions during this session. Chair, as we draw closer to 2030, we must take stock of our accomplishments, reflect on challenges to the advancement of social development, and reiterate the need to scale up efforts to achieve the objectives set forth in the Copenhagen Declaration and Programme of Action, the Doha Political Declaration, and the SDGs. These provide comprehensive frameworks for advancing implementation and accelerating progress in social development. Eradicating hunger and poverty, reducing inequalities, ensuring access to decent work, education, and social protection are some of the fundamental elements that guide our social development framework. CARICOM's own efforts to address these challenges are guided by the region's human resource development 2030 strategy. As a region that knows all too well the devastating effects of climate change and how it can contribute to widening inequalities. CARICOM reiterates its commitment to continue building the resilience of our people and our region. CARICOM remains committed to a people-centered approach to development to ensure that noone is left behind. Notwithstanding, effective implementation of commitments are hampered by resource constraints. CARICOM therefore reiterates the need for international cooperation aimed at building resilience, reducing inequalities, and alleviating poverty. Chair CARICOM reaffirms its steadfast commitment to the full and accelerated implementation of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, and all other relevant international frameworks aimed at achieving gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls. The full, equal, and meaningful participation of women is indispensable to the realization of sustainable development. including in such critical areas as peacebuilding, conflict prevention and climate action. We remain deeply concerned by the persistent and disproportionate challenges faced by women and girls, particularly regarding poverty, gender-based violence and unequal access to decent employment and economic opportunity. We welcome the adoption of the resolution on the revitalization of the Commission on the Status of Women. which reaffirms the Commission's central role in follow-up to the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, and seeks to strengthen its effectiveness in accelerating implementation, bridging the gap between global commitments and lived realities, and advancing the rights and empowerment of all women and girls. CARICOM urges the international community to translate commitments into concrete action. This requires increased, predictable and adequately targeted international financing to address the needs and priorities of women and girls, as well as strengthened policies, legislative reform and renewed political will. Only through sustained implementation and accountability can the international community deliver meaningful and lasting progress. Chair CARICOM reaffirms the pivotal role of the Human Rights Council in advancing the promotion and protection of all human rights and fundamental freedoms. While awaiting the forthcoming report of the Council, CARICOM underscores the importance of ensuring that its work is carried out in an equitable, transparent, and non-discriminatory manner, including through initiatives that enhance the meaningful engagement of small island developing states. CARICOM further highlights the inherent interlinkages between sustainable development, climate resilience, and the full and effective enjoyment of human rights for all. CARICOM maintains that every child has the right to grow up in an environment where their dignity, safety, and well-being are protected. This includes the right to education, healthcare, and family life, as well as protection from violence and exploitation, and the opportunity to participate in decisions that affect their lives. These rights must be upheld without discrimination, regardless of a child's background or circumstances. Children's lives are becoming increasingly connected to artificial intelligence and digital technologies. Digital tools can create valuable opportunities for learning, communication, and access to essential services, but they can also expose children to new risks, including privacy violations, online harm, and exploitation. It is therefore essential that children's rights and safety remain at the center of how these technologies are developed, used, and regulated. Ultimately, protecting children's rights is a shared responsibility that requires action from our governments, local communities, and international organizations. This means ensuring that children's voices are heard and that policies, services, and technologies reflect their best interests. By investing in and protecting children's rights today, we can help build safer and more equal societies for generations to come. Chair, CARICOM remains committed to the promotion, preservation, and transmission of culture and heritage across generations. In this regard, we look forward to CARIFEST, the Caribbean Festival of Arts in 2027. This will provide an important platform to showcase the diverse cultural expressions of the Caribbean, including music, dance, visual arts, literature, and other creative forms. CARICOM also welcomes the resolution adopted last month on enhancing the participation of indigenous peoples, representatives, and institutions in meetings of relevant UN bodies on issues affecting them. We view this as an important step towards strengthening the meaningful, effective and inclusive participation of Indigenous Peoples in multilateral processes and ensuring that their perspectives and priorities are reflected in decisions that affect their communities. CARICOM encourages governments, intergovernmental and non-governmental organizations, the private sector and other relevant stakeholders to continue supporting and contributing to the UN Voluntary Fund for Indigenous Peoples. Such support is essential to ensuring that Indigenous Peoples can meaningfully participate in the international processes that shape their future, while preserving and advancing the knowledge, traditions, and stories of our ancestors that continue to define and enrich our identity today. Chair, this year we commemorate the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action. As the most relevant and comprehensive international framework for addressing racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance, the DDPA must continue to underpin our efforts to create a more just and equitable world. On this anniversary, We must regrettably acknowledge that racism, discrimination, and xenophobia remain pervasive worldwide, now intensified by digital technologies and AI systems. Addressing these contemporary manifestations requires collaboration among various stakeholders, but most importantly, the political will to prioritize the elimination of racism and racial discrimination from digital spaces. Addressing these challenges requires us to also confront the root causes of racism. The historical injustices perpetrated against people of African descent, particularly through colonialism and the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans, are the foundational causes of modern racism. Without meaningful redress for these crimes, true justice and healing will evade the descendants of victims, deepening systemic exclusion and inequality. CARICOM launched in July of this year its revised 10-point plan for reparatory justice, building on the previous plan and providing a comprehensive framework for repairing the legacies of the period of colonization, native genocide, and the transatlantic trafficking and enslaved Africans in our countries. It acknowledges the persistent ills faced by descendants of the victims and sets a clear path for providing remedy. including through a formal apology, restitution, compensation, and rehabilitation. CARICOM believes that it is well overdue for the international community to confront and adequately address the issue of reparatory justice for people of African descent. CARICOM reiterates our support for the work of the Permanent Forum on People of African Descent whose fifth session earlier this year placed a central focus on expanding human rights under the second International Decade for People of African Descent. We believe that the second International Decade must be more impactful than the first and must truly deliver recognition, justice, and development for people of African descent. Chair, CARICOM remains deeply concerned by the persistently high levels of violence and transnational crime in the region. which are driven by the illicit proliferation of firearms, trafficking in persons, other forms of organized transnational crimes, and emerging threats. CARICOM therefore reaffirms its commitment to a comprehensive response, integrating public safety, security development, and fair justice perspectives within the Caribbean, supported by regional mechanisms such as CARICOM IMPACS, and the Caribbean Community Action Plan for Social Development and Crime Prevention. CARICOM further welcomes the technical cooperation provided by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime in advancing regional security priorities, including efforts to address firearms trafficking, maritime and border security, drug trafficking, cybercrime, corruption, and crimes affecting the environment. CARICOM particularly welcomes the launch of the UNODC Enforce project, which supports the implementation of the arms embargo on Haiti and seeks to strengthen regional cooperation and enforcement capacity. Continued, predictable, and demand-driven technical assistance from UNODC remains essential to enabling Caribbean states, including small island developing states, to build resilient, accountable, and human rights-compliant criminal justice systems strengthen cross-border cooperation, and respond effectively to the evolving threats posed by transnational organized crime. CARICOM also recognizes the direct correlation between the prevalence of gun crimes and trafficking in narcotics due to the many shared routes that facilitate the parallel flow of drugs and illegal firearms through our borders. We note in the report of the Secretary General the acknowledgement of the growing complexity of the global drug challenge. Of particular concern for CARICOM is the expansion of cocaine trafficking, other synthetic and new psychoactive drugs whose movement relies heavily on maritime routes. The increasing infiltration of these substances into our societies has resulted in a growing popularity among and consumption by our youth, heightening their health risks and the risk of them choosing a life of crime. while significantly undermining efforts.

I thank the distinguished permanent representative of Jamaica on behalf of CARICOM. I invite the distinguished permanent representative of Cuba on behalf of the Group of States to be followed by Ireland. The distinguished permanent representative of Cuba, you have the floor.

Thank you, President. Mr. President, I have the honor of delivering the statement on behalf of Belarus, Burundi, China, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Iran, Lao People's Democratic Republic, Mali, Nicaragua, Niger, State of Palestine, Russian Federation, Uganda, Zimbabwe, and my own country, Cuba. To save some time, I'll read an abridged version. The official version in English will be available in the UN Journal. allow us to convey our best wishes to you and to other members of the Bureau. We look forward to working together in an active and constructive manner throughout this session. Mr. President, we attach a supreme value to the promotion and protection of all human rights, both individual and collective, without distinction of levels or categories. And we also consider that their protection and promotion must be enhanced on the basis of dialogue and cooperation and in adherence to the principles of impartiality, objectivity, transparency, non-selectivity, non-politization, and non-confrontation, taking into account the respect for sovereignty and non-intervention in internal matters of states as set out in the Charter of the UN and within the framework of equality and mutual respect. All actors of the UN human rights system, including treaty bodies, the Human Rights Council, its special procedures, and the Universal Periodic Review, as well as the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and other relevant departments of the UN Secretariat, should continue to work on the basis of multilateralism, cooperation, respect, and dialogue. Achieving this goal while preserving the credibility and the integrity of the UN human rights system is only possible through a constructive dialogue and cooperation with States. The UN human rights machinery must be protected from politicization at all times. Mr. President, we live in an extremely challenging and dangerous international context. Threats to international peace and security are on the rise. Attempts are being made to legalize flagrant violations of the UN Charter and policies of domination are promoted, policies which threaten social development, the right to self-determination, and the promotion and protection of human rights around the world. The exacerbation of trends that promote unilateralism and divisionism weakens the United Nations and undermines a truly democratic, fair, inclusive, and equitable international order. In this complex context, we reiterate our deepest concern and condemnation at the ongoing acts of violence committed by Israel against the Palestinian people, particularly in Gaza, including its systematic resort to forced displacement and starvation, as well as the deliberate destruction of civilian and critical infrastructures. Israel's ongoing violations of the ceasefire reached in Gaza are unacceptable. We renew our call to end the ongoing occupation, violence, bloodshed, and the prevailing cycle of impunity against Palestinians. A serious multilateral effort within the framework of the United Nations is essential to ensure, among other aspects, safe and unhindered humanitarian access for those in a situation of desperate need as well as the mandate and work of UNRWA in the occupied Palestinian territory. We continue to advocate for a just, lasting and comprehensive solution to the question of Palestine, in line with relevant UN resolutions and the two-state solution. We condemn in the strongest possible terms the heinous attacks perpetrated by the United States and Israel against the Islamic Republic of Iran on 28 February 2026, which caused the death of innocent civilians, including women and children. We stress that these reprehensible attacks constitute flagrant violations of the Charter of the United Nations, international law, including international human rights law, and international humanitarian law. They also grossly violate the fundamental principles of sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the prohibition of the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity and political independence of states. Dialogue, good neighborliness, and relations based on peace, friendship, and cooperation must prevail in the region, Mr. President. The political, economic, social and cultural diversity of today's world constitutes a value that must be preserved and respected on the basis of multilateralism and the continued promotion of a culture of peace, intercultural and interreligious dialogue, nonviolence and the fight against hate speech and disinformation as indispensable tools for strengthening the values enshrined both in the Charter as well as in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. In this context, we strongly oppose any form of collective punishment against certain nations as a result of the freely expressed will of their peoples. This includes the so-called cancel culture, which negatively affects the realization of their rights in the spheres of education, culture, sport, science, religion and other relevant fields and leads to social exclusion. We reiterate our categorical rejection of double standards in the field of human rights, and we express our grave concern over the continued proliferation of mechanisms and procedures that pretend to conduct impartial assessments of the human rights situations in specific states without the due consent or participation of the concerned states. We condemn the establishment of any mechanism of this kind on the basis of bilateral agreements with states other than states concerned and under the pretext of providing technical assistance to third parties. We reiterate the need to rely on credible and verified sources to take into account member states efforts when it comes to human rights, as well as the impact of external challenges. We also reaffirm our strong condemnation to the application of unilateral coercive measures, especially against several of our countries, which dramatically affect the full enjoyment of human rights for more than one third of humanity, preventing and hindering access, among others, to food, medicines and medical treatment or equipment, financial services, education, technological advances, sources of energy, among other fundamental goods and services. Allow us to be clear. It is not just contradictory, but also immoral that some governments pretend to portray themselves as advocates and alleged defenders of human rights, while at the same time their deliberate and systemic policies, especially the application of unilateral coercive measures, cause mass violations to the human rights of billions of people around the world on a daily basis. This is simply unacceptable. We reiterate our strong condemnation of the illegal economic, commercial, and financial blockade imposed by the United States against Cuba. tightened with an energy siege, which continues to have devastating consequences for the Cuban people. Once again, we urge States to refrain from enacting and implementing them and to lift any unilateral coercive economic, financial, or commercial measure that could impede the full achievement of economic and social development, given the negative impact of these measures on the full enjoyment and realization of all human rights and the achievement of the SDGs. Mr. President, we also express our grave concern at the persistent world drug problem, which must be addressed in full respect of the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations and the sovereignty of States. We reaffirmed our firm commitment to the international drug control regime. We underlined that migration is not a crime and that the rights and the dignity of migrants must be respected in line with relevant national and international obligations. We recognize that external factors, such as the systematic application of unilateral coercive measures, are one of the main drivers of migration. We reaffirm that migration, including voluntary return, must be safe, orderly, and conducted in full respect of the dignity of migrants in order to prevent crimes related to trafficking in persons. We also stress that migration policies must be rooted in solidarity, international cooperation, and the full respect for the sovereignty of states and international law. while we strongly reject the persecution and stigmatization of migrants, particularly in Western countries. Mr. President, we condemn and reject systemic racism and racial discrimination, xenophobia and any related form of intolerance, and we reaffirm that human rights belong to everyone without distinction of any kind, as enshrined in Article 2 of the Universal Declaration on Human Rights, we categorically reject the resurgence of tendencies that promote the idea of superiority among human beings. This includes fascism, Nazism, neo-Nazism, and any form of racial exceptionalism. We reaffirm that the right to development is an inalienable human right. It belongs to every human being and all peoples, and it must be fully realized without discrimination of any kind. We call for the timely finalization of an International Covenant on the Right to Development as a legally binding instrument on the basis of the proposal made by the Human Rights Council. The adoption of this covenant would be a historic step to rectify the global asymmetry, reaffirming the right of developing countries to pursue their own development paths free from coercion, and ensuring that international cooperation is based on equity, solidarity, and shared responsibility. We insist that there shall be no other option but dialogue, cooperation, engagement, and national ownership in each process that is truly aimed at strengthening human rights at both the national and international levels, while we also reaffirm our firm our staunch determination to continue working in an active and constructive manner towards the enhancement of the efficacy and credibility of the UN human rights system, as well as to preserve, promote, and defend the prevalence and validity of the Charter of the United Nations, both in its letter and spirit. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished permanent representative of Cuba. and I will pass the floor in a moment to Ireland, followed by Germany. Distinguished Permanent Representative of Ireland, you have the floor.

I wish to you and your colleagues for the time ahead. Chair, I have the honour to deliver the cross-regional joint statement on reprisals for cooperation with the United Nations on behalf of the following member states: Albania, Andorra, Antigua and Barbuda, Armenia, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Brazil, Bulgaria, Cabo Verde, Canada, Chile, Costa Rica, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Georgia, Portugal, the Republic of Korea, Romania, Germany, Greece, Guatemala, Hungary, Iceland, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Mexico, Moldova, Monaco, Montenegro, Myanmar, Netherlands, New Zealand, North Macedonia, Norway, Panama, Poland, Spain, Sweden, San Marino, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Africa, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Ukraine, as well as our colleagues from Uruguay, the European Union, and my own country, Ireland. The participation of civil society actors and human rights defenders is integral to advancing the work of the United Nations and our collective commitments to uphold human rights, accelerate implementation of the SDGs, and build more peaceful, equal, and just societies. Their safe and meaningful participation brings expertise, transparency, accountability, and lived experiences to the heart of global policymaking and ensures that our efforts are responsive, effective, and grounded in the realities that individuals face. This increases UN credibility and effectiveness by contributing to more informed and inclusive decision-making. It also empowers communities, enhances good governance, leads to greater impact on the ground, and amplifies the voices of those left further behind. At a time of continued and increasing threat against civic space, we reaffirm our collective commitment to protect, support, and ensure the safe, meaningful, and unhindered engagement of individuals and groups with the United Nations, including its representatives and mechanisms in the field of human rights. As Member States, we bear the primary responsibility for preventing and addressing reprisals against those who cooperate with the United Nations. We condemn in the strongest possible terms all acts of intimidation or reprisal, whether online or offline, perpetrated by state and non-state actors against those who seek to cooperate or who have cooperated with the United Nations. Chair, we welcome the latest report by the Secretary General on reprisals, as well as his presentation by Assistant Secretary General Claudia Fuentes Julio to the third committee later this month. The report's findings are, again, deeply troubling. They demonstrate that reprisals remain widespread, persistent, and in some contexts, increasingly sophisticated. Civic space is shrinking. Individuals and organizations face criminalization, harassment, threats and attacks, as well as administrative restrictions and hurdles, simply for cooperating or seeking to cooperate with the UN. Repeated and longstanding instances point to broader efforts to control and restrict civic space and deter engagement with the UN. The report also notes the severe effects on family members, on witnesses, and on survivors. The instrumentalisation of legal and regulatory frameworks to counter transnational crime, as well as the continued misuse of counter-terrorism, cybercrime and national security laws to restrict the engagement of civil society organisations and human rights defenders with the UN, as set out in the report, is also of great concern. Such oppressive misuse of legal and regulatory frameworks undermines international human rights obligations and weakens the multilateral system on which we all depend. It is especially alarming that more than half the States referenced in the Secretary-General's report applied, amended or enacted laws that criminalised or further restricted cooperation with the United Nations. We acknowledge with concern that the extent and instances of reprisals reported do not reflect the true breadth and scope of the issue. In many instances, individuals resort to self-censorship, anonymous engagement or even cease engagement with the UN because of a climate of fear and intimidation and concerns for their safety and that of their families and communities. Chair, the report also confirms that transnational repression is on the rise. This appalling reality requires concerted action on the part of Member States. Reports of arbitrary detention, criminal charges, in absentia trials, physical attacks, intimidation, confiscation of property and passports, and movement restrictions demonstrate the increasingly cross-border nature of reprisals and intimidation. We are deeply concerned by the increasing role of digital technology in enabling transnational repression through intimidation, surveillance, harassment, coordinated disinformation campaigns and reprisals. Chair, rising instances of reprisals not take place in a vacuum, nor do they only affect civil society and human rights defenders. Targeting of independent mandate holders, representatives from staff of international organizations, and judges for implementing their mandates aimed at upholding human rights obligations and standards, investigating violations, and promoting accountability is completely unacceptable. Such actions also have a deterrent effect on individuals and groups seeking to cooperate with them. We affirm our unwavering support for those who seek to work towards accountability for violations of international law. We are concerned about the impact of restrictions and denials of access to UN personnel, including in the context of peace operations and against those who cooperate with or brief the Security Council. Such actions weaken the ability of the UN to fulfil its responsibilities and deprive it of critical information required to respond effectively to emerging risks and crises. We are further concerned about the disproportionate impact of reprisals on certain groups. Women human rights defenders often face gender-based forms of intimidation and violence. Indigenous peoples also face particular risks, including in the context of lands, territories and resources, the environment, biodiversity and climate, as do young people, LGBTI persons and those advocating for non-discrimination and equal rights. It is the responsibility of Member States to take concrete action to prevent and address acts of reprisals, including acts of transnational repression. We call on all States to fully comply with their obligations under international law, including international human rights law. All Member States must refrain from unlawfully or arbitrarily surveilling, harassing or targeting individuals or groups for cooperating with the UN, including through the use of digital technologies. Where reports of reprisals, including transnational repression, arise, States should conduct prompt, thorough and impartial investigations, ensure accountability for those responsible and provide adequate safeguarding and protection mechanisms for those at risk. We welcome the good practices identified in the Secretary-General's report and call on Member States to engage actively with the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights to ensure meaningful and safe engagement of civil society and human rights defenders with the UN, including through the political and financial support necessary for the Office to fulfil its mandate effectively. We call on Member States to promote the meaningful and safe participation of civil society actors and human rights defenders in UN processes, including through support for access and appropriate modalities, and to push back against any efforts to further diminish their participation. We welcome the Secretary-General's commitment to placing the prevention of and response to reprisals at the core of the United Nations' work, in line with the organization's zero-tolerance approach and the UN Agenda for Protection. We encourage his successor to maintain and to strengthen this commitment. In line with the zero-tolerance approach, we call for tangible steps to put safeguards and support mechanisms in place for those who are implementing their mandates or are cooperating with the UN, including with the Security Council. We urge the UN to take further measures to further strengthen its institutional response to ensuring that robust systems are in place to identify, document, report and follow up on reports of reprisals, regardless of how long such incidents have been reported, through designated focal points, as well as sustainably resourcing their work. A strong and vibrant civil society is indispensable in our collective efforts to respect, promote and protect human rights and ensure accountability for violations at the domestic, regional and international levels. As civic space continues to shrink, safeguarding meaningful civil society participation with and at the UN is a human rights imperative, an essential element of effective and inclusive multinational action, and a responsibility shared by us all. Those who raise concerns, provide accountability, and expose violations and abuses must be protected, not persecuted. As Member States, we will do all that we can to ensure that those who engage with the United Nations can do so safely, freely, and without fear. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished Permanent Representative of Ireland. I will pass the floor to Germany, followed by Portugal. Distinguished Representative of Germany, you have the floor.

Chair, this year marks the 60th anniversary of the adoption of two core human rights treaties, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Sixty years later, their promise remains as vital as it was in 1966. Every person is entitled to the full enjoyment of their human rights and fundamental freedoms, every day, everywhere. Human rights are universal. They unite us, transcending the different political, economic, and cultural circumstances under which we live. Germany is a strong supporter of the UN human rights system. This is why Germany is seeking election to the Human Rights Council for 2027 to 2029. The history of our own country has shown what happens when human rights are systematically denied, when the foundations of freedom and peace are destroyed by terror. We are aware of our responsibility to stand up for human rights wherever they are violated or challenged. both at home and around the world. The full realization of human rights is essential to human dignity, peaceful and inclusive societies, and sustainable development. Allow me to highlight four thematic points. First, Germany is deeply alarmed by the sharp surge in the use of the death penalty by only a few remaining states worldwide, including the application of the death penalty in relation to drug-related offenses. There is no conclusive evidence that the death penalty contributes to curbing or preventing drug trafficking more than other types of punishment. We remain equally concerned about extrajudicial, summary, or arbitrary executions. Second, we are deeply concerned by threats, intimidation, and reprisals, including acts of transnational repression, aimed at silencing voices beyond national borders. The protection of human rights also depends on those who have the courage to defend them, human rights defenders, journalists, and civil society representatives. They give a voice to those who might otherwise go unheard. They expose violations and strengthen accountability and contribute to a more open, resilient, inclusive, and democratic societies. Thank you, Madam Chair. Allow me to congratulate you on your appointment and wish you every success in steering this important committee. Austria aligns itself with the statement of the European Union and the joint statement delivered on behalf of a cross-regional group of countries on reprisals. Madam Chair, as our Secretary General stated earlier this year, when human rights fail and fall, everything else tumbles. Peace, development, social cohesion, trust, and solidarity. Human rights are under severe pressure today. our world faces transformational change and a surge in armed conflict. Polarization is deepening, civic space is shrinking, and far too often, international law and respect for human rights are treated as optional. Our response cannot be selective. I would like to mention in this context that we also welcome the High Commissioner's initiative launching the new Global Alliance for Human Rights, mobilizing actors from all sectors, regions, and generations. Second, we must address the human rights implications of unprecedented technological advancements. Automated drone systems have profound consequences for civilians. AI-driven capabilities are exploited to recruit children for their use in cyber operations. Online platforms are misused to spread hatred and technology-facilitated gender-based violence. As others have pointed out, this cannot be let go. Digital surveillance can endanger fundamental freedoms and pose threats to independent media. To harness the opportunities of modern technology, but also regulate and prevent its misuse, we must adopt a human rights-based approach to the development of IA and digital governance. And dear colleagues, distinguished delegates, we count on your support and cooperation for this text, including co-sponsorship. Nearly 60,000 community health workers remain the backbone of our primary health backbone ecosystem. Madam Chair and colleagues, as we begin a new session of this committee, Rwanda looks forward to engaging constructively across all agendas and working through with all delegations in the spirit of dialogue, cooperation and mutual respect. towards a successful decision. And thank you, Madam Chair and colleagues, for listening. Thank you.
