Harmful practices such as female genital mutilation and early child and forced marriage, together with every other manifestation of gender-based violence, constitute grave violations of human rights and a major obstacle to achieving gender equality. We call upon all States to guarantee survivors effective access to justice and to address the root causes of such violence in order to prevent its recurrence. At the national level, we are proud to announce that Italy has introduced femicide as a distinct criminal offence, punishable by life imprisonment alongside strengthened victim support mechanisms and measures to promote women's economic independence, which are essential factors in enabling women to break free from cycles of violence and abuse. Italy's commitment extends beyond the prevention of violence to the removal of structural obstacles that continue to hinder women's participation in decision-making and professional advancement. Italy currently co-chairs, together with the Philippines, the network of focal points on women, peace and security, whose eighth capital-level meeting was convened in Rome this past June. This reflects our continued commitment to advancing gender equality and to ensuring that women can fully and meaningfully contribute to the decision-making processes. This commitment is all the more important in the context of today's unprecedented humanitarian crisis, which continue to have a disproportionate impact on women and girls. Italy's longstanding efforts to promote women's empowerment and gender equality are rooted in the recognition that meaningful and effective inclusion of women in all areas of public life is essential to fostering lasting change, strengthening peaceful coexistence, and building more inclusive societies. Italy firmly believes in the key contribution of youth to multilateralism and international cooperation, and it's committed to ensuring that youth participation is not only a matter of principle, but is supported by concrete institutional structures and measurable action. Since 2017, Italy has implemented a United Nations Youth Delegate Program, providing young people with a direct channel to participate in international policymaking. Since 2018, this commitment has also been reflected in the establishment of a National Youth Council, a formal advisory body bringing together youth organizations from across the country. Building on these efforts, Italy became the second country in Europe to adopt a National Action Plan on Youth, Peace and Security. The plan for the period of 26-29 includes concrete measures such as a dedicated funding line to support youth participation in international peace and security processes, an increase in the number of Italian UN youth delegates, as well as the establishment of a permanent youth forum and foreign policy. Its implementation is overseen by a national steering committee and on the WPS agenda, with periodic reporting and evaluation against the five pillars of the WPS agenda. This monitoring framework helps ensure accountability and assess progress towards concrete outcome, ensuring that commitments to youth participation are translated into sustained institutional action and measurable results. The protection of children in armed conflict remains a matter of grave concern to Italy, despite the three decades of normative progress within the United Nations. Recent reports point to an alarming increase in grave violations against children, including attacks on schools and hospitals, recruitment, sexual violence, and denial of humanitarian access, compounded by the growing use of autonomous aerial systems and artificial intelligence in battlefield targeting. Children must never be regarded as an acceptable cost of armed conflict. Italy therefore reiterates its call for the full implementation of Security Council Resolution 2601 and for the broadest endorsement of the Safe School Declaration. Similarly, violence against children in all its form must be eradicated wherever it occurs. Italy is firmly committed to ensuring that the rights of children, especially those in situation of vulnerability, are protected everywhere and that every child can grow up free from abuse, trafficking, exploitation, or other forms of violence, including in digital environments. Madam Chair, several of these concerns converge in the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. Women represent barely one in five artificial intelligence professionals worldwide and hold fewer than one in seven senior leadership positions in the sector. At the same time, the growing use of artificial intelligence can amplify online abuse targeting women and girls while reinforcing gender stereotypes and existing patterns of structural discrimination. Children are also exposed to these emerging risks, including persuasive disinformation, misleading deep fake content, and the potential misuse of generative AI systems. Italy calls for strengthened international cooperation to ensure that the governance of artificial intelligence remains firmly grounded in human rights and effectively addresses the specific risks faced by women, girls, and children. The fight against all forms of discrimination remains central to our human rights agenda. We believe that any form of discrimination is fundamentally incompatible with the universality and indivisibility of human rights. Italy has given concrete expression to this principle through its third national action plan for the rights and inclusion of persons with disabilities, grounded on the importance of ensuring persons with disabilities greater autonomy in decisions concerning their lives. In addition, Italy has undertaken a broader reform, establishing a national guarantor authority for the right of person with disabilities and introducing the life project, conceived to overcome the fragmentation between healthcare and social services. The same principle informs Italy's approach to the aging population, whose needs call for coordinated policy and sustained investment in lifelong learning, so that all the works are not left behind by the green and digital transition. Lastly, we wish to underscore the importance of culture and dialogue in fostering mutual understanding, respect, tolerance, and in promoting human rights. Cultural diversity should be valued as a source of enrichment for all humanity, while fully preserving the universality and indivisibility of human rights. At the same time, cultural heritage must be safeguarded, particularly in situations of armed conflict, where cultural sites and traditions are too often deliberately targeted. In this regard, Italy has taken a concrete step by co-chairing, since September 2026, together with Mexico, the Group of Friends for Culture, working to give culture a more central place on the United Nations agenda, including through the responsible use of artificial intelligence to document and safeguard cultural heritage. Madam Chair, Italy stands ready to work with all Member States in a spirit of dialogue and cooperation to address these pressing challenges and to ensure that human dignity and rights are upheld for all. I thank you, Madam Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Italy. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of China.

Chair, colleagues, I would like to congratulate Ambassador Larsen on his assumption of the chairmanship of the Third Committee. I'm confident that under his leadership, this session will be a great success. Respecting, protecting, and realizing human rights is a shared aspiration of all countries, and peoples. Looking back, we have witnessed both progress in the international human rights endeavor and the persistence of injustice, intolerance, and instability. We've also seen the continued evolution of the international human rights system alongside the serious strain it faces from unilateralism and power politics. The international landscape is undergoing the most complex and profound changes since the Second World War. The international human rights endeavor faces unprecedented risks and challenges. In particular, imbalances between the two categories of human rights have deepened. The politicization of human rights has intensified. Double standards are increasingly prevalent. These trends not only erode the fundamental values of human rights, but also seriously undermine the authority and effectiveness of multilateral human rights mechanisms. widening the governance deficit and hindering effective response to real-world challenges. What kind of human rights governance system does the world need? How can countries participate in and advance global human rights governance? We must build consensus and make choices that stand the test of practice, the people, and history. A year ago, President Xi Jinping solemnly put forward the Global Governance Initiative, charting a course for addressing current global challenges and providing China's answer to reforming and improving global human rights governance. On numerous occasions in multilateral human rights fora, China has called for upholding the vision of a community with a shared future, uniting under the banner of the UN and working together to steer global human rights governance back on course. First, we must uphold fairness and justice and stay firmly on the right political course. All countries, regardless of size, strength and wealth, are equal and have the right to independently choose their own path of human rights development and to participate, make decisions and benefit on an equal footing in international human rights affairs. We must uphold the fundamental principles of international law, including sovereign equality and non-interference in internal affairs, as well as the basic norms governing international address human rights issues in a fair, objective, and a non-selective manner, reject double standards and the imposition of one's will on others, oppose politicization, instrumentalization, and the weaponization of human rights, and strengthen the international community's confidence and resolve to uphold the multilateral human rights system. Second, we must put people first and uphold the right values. People are at the heart of human rights. Effectively addressing the most pressing and practical concerns of people's lives and development and enabling people in all countries to lead better lives is the starting point and ultimate goal of the international human rights endeavor. In the face of global turmoil, we must resolve international disputes and hotspot issues through peaceful means, oppose violent conflict, and protect human rights through security. With development in mind, we must narrow the North-South divide, jointly promote inclusive development, and advance human rights through development. In a new multipolar landscape, we must eliminate barriers and prejudices, deepen dialogue among civilizations and people-to-people exchanges, and advance human rights through cooperation. Third, we must practice multilateralism and focus on action. Without a stable international order, there can be no effective human rights protection. Without genuine multilateral cooperation, human rights governance will remain empty rhetoric. We must support reform to strengthen multilateral human rights institutions and enhance the representation and the voice of countries in the Global South. We must ensure balanced progress on the three pillars, focus on key issues. develop a common agenda, and actively address new challenges related to emerging technologies, climate change, and public health security. Turn commitment to multilateralism into action and build a more just and equitable global human rights governance system. Chair, colleagues, Today marks the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China. This year also marks the 105th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China and the 55th anniversary of the restoration of the People's Republic of China's lawful seat in the UN. History bears witness to China's practice of respecting and protecting human rights, and its vision and steadfast efforts to build a community with a shared future for humanity. We uphold the belief that a happy life is the greatest human right, and we continue to develop and improve whole-process people's democracy, ensuring that the benefits of Chinese modernization are shared more extensively and equitably by all. We promote the common prosperity and development of all ethnic groups through the rule of law, and protect the rights of women, children, older persons, and persons with disabilities to equal participation and development. We advance green and low carbon development and promote people's all-round development through digital and intelligent technologies. We advocate shared values for all humanity, implement the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative, the Global Civilization Initiative, and the Global Governance Initiative, deepen international human rights cooperation, and inject strong impetus into to building a better world together. China has consistently demonstrated through concrete actions as a responsible major country that progress in the cause of human rights must be supported by development, safeguarded by good governance, and advanced through cooperation. China calls for strengthening the development pillar, better supporting the UN's social development agenda, increasing investment in economic, social, and cultural rights, and the right to development, and stepping up support for countries in the global south. We will take the fifth anniversary of the Global Development Initiative as a new starting point to strengthen international cooperation in development and promote stronger, greener, and healthier development worldwide. China calls for accelerating a new process toward gender equality and women's comprehensive development, fully leveraging women's leading role and the transformative power, and building a broader platform for cooperation among women from all countries. We stand ready to work with all parties to fully implement the outcomes of the Global Women's Summit held in Beijing last October and to further advance the global cause of women's development. China calls for eliminating all forms of racism and racial discrimination. promoting inclusive coexistence, mutual exchange and learning among different countries, peoples, civilizations and religions, and ensuring that all people enjoy equal dignity and rights. The sovereignty and national dignity of all countries must be protected and respected. We support the just cause of the Palestinian people. in pursuing their legitimate national cause, national rights, and a call on the international community to make sustained efforts to advance historical justice and reparations for Africans, people of African descent, and indigenous peoples. China calls on all parties to uphold a vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit, strengthen Solidarity and collaboration oppose unilateralism, promote international cooperation and global governance in AI, public health, refugees and migrants, and combating drugs and crime. We attach importance to protecting the rights and interests of specific groups, including women, children, youth, and the persons with disability and older persons, so as to better promote human well-being. Chair, colleagues, good principles keep abreast of the times. The trend toward a multipolar world and greater democracy in international relations is unstoppable, and our times call for a fairer and more equitable global governance system. China has always been a force for stability in a turbulent world, a steadfast force for shared development, and a force for progress in an era of transformation. China will continue to champion multilateralism, promote the spirit of unity and cooperation, and further contribute to global progress through its own governance. We will work to ensure the fruits of reforming the global governance system and building a community with a shared future for humanity bring greater benefits to people around the world. Thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of China. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sweden.

Thank you, Chair. As we gather here today, we are preparing for weeks of negotiations, discussions, and debates. Weeks where we will disagree and compromise, but where we will also come together. In honor of the promise we made here in New York, as stated in the Universal Declaration on Human Rights, almost 80 years ago. The promise that human rights should be effectively recognized and observed by all member states. I would like to take this opportunity to remind us not only of what human rights are and the many ways that they can be violated, but also on what they can build. Respect for human rights creates prosperity, foster trust, and lay the foundation for security. Because when human rights are not respected or protected, societies are not safe and not just, and the risk of conflict and aggression rise. Around the world, we witness the blatant disregard of human rights. In Ukraine, Russia continues its brutal and illegal war of aggression and deliberate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure. The mounting evidence of Russia's violations of international law is appalling. At the same time, the authoritarian Russian regime effectively suppresses the right of freedom of expression and opinion within their own borders, as demonstrated by the so-called Duma elections, marked by severe restrictions on opposition voices and independent participation. In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, settler violence against Palestinians is escalating as Israel continues its settlement policy in clear violation of international law. At the same time, humanitarian aid and NGOs and independent media's access to Gaza is effectively restricted or denied. while the continued refusal of Hamas to disarm and leave power constitutes a significant obstacle to peace. In Iran, peaceful protests have been followed by violent repression and a dramatic and deeply concerning increase in the use of the death penalty. And from Sudan, we hear horrifying reports of sexual and gender-based violence being used as a method of war during a humanitarian crisis. I could go on, but the pattern is clear. Human rights violations are followed by increasing insecurities around the world. And where human rights are not respected, the prospects of peace is bleak. It also goes hand in hand with a growing pressure on democracies around the world, limiting people's ability to participate, organize, and speak freely, and hold those in power to account. Human rights and democracy are mutually reinforcing. Democracy provides the foundation through which human rights can be protected and advanced, why it remains one of our strongest safeguards against conflict, instability and insecurity. At the same time, respect for human rights is essential for democracy to function, ensuring the freedoms and safeguards on which democratic societies depend. This is why I say Human rights are not only values, they are legal commitments, but even more so, they are fundamental building blocks of a more secure and prosperous world, a world which we all have an interest to create. In the coming weeks, it is our duty to fulfill at least part of this task, an overwhelming task it may seem, but possible if we come together. I say this with hope because I dare to believe. I believe that we, the majority of states represented today, remain committed to the cause. And I believe that we can ultimately agree that we are willing to put in the work to come together in the interest of a more secure and prosperous world, where human dignity is not only a value or a moral imperative, but a guarantee. Madam Chair. Of course, the close interconnection between human rights, security, and prosperity is no news to an organization such as the UN, built around furthering those very objectives. Still, it seems that now, more than ever, you need a reminder of what that still means. The UN was founded on three pillars that can and will not be separated, three pillars guiding our work, closely intertwined and mutually reinforcing. Because only when human rights are respected can peace, security and sustainable development be achieved. Yet one of these pillars remains severely underfinanced, and we have seen the negative effects of a liquidity crisis. And at this moment in time, when violent crises arise and the need for protection from gross human rights violations and abuses continue to grow, The UN human rights pillar urgently needs to be strengthened, not weakened. Adequate, predictable and sustainable funding is a prerequisite for its functioning, because it is in fact an investment in our security. The Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, the treaty bodies and the special procedures, including the mandates of the fact-finding missions and independent experts, together they develop norms and standards, they investigate and they collect evidence on human rights violations and abuses, and review States' compliance with the human rights treaties that we have agreed on. They translate our shared human rights commitments into action and ensure accountability. and they must be given the resources and the independence they need to fulfill their mandates, free from political interference. Because the impact of the human rights pillar goes far beyond the meeting rooms here in New York or in Geneva. It helps train judges and police officers, supports legal reforms, protects human rights defenders at risk, contribute to the release of arbitrarily detained individuals, strengthens national institutions and documents violation to to ensure future accountability. In this way, it delivers tangible results on the ground and improves the lives of so many people, far beyond the words that we agree or disagree on, on paper. Ensuring accountability for perpetrators and justice for victims of widespread human rights violations and abuses is an important part of this pillar. We recognise in this regard the vital role of the International Criminal Court. Of course, we as Member States must also take our shared responsibility for the functioning of the pillar to protect this crucial work. We encourage all Member States to pay assessed contributions in full on time and without conditions, and to contribute to the rationalization and efficiency process here in New York and in Geneva. But we also expect UN leadership, including the next Secretary-General, to fully stand behind the equal value and functioning of all three pillars. We need an effective UN as a cornerstone of multilateralism and human rights. The UN80 reforms should enable a UN that is better funded, less fragmented and stronger on both delivery and norms. Let me also take this opportunity to welcome the High Commissioner's recent initiative, the Global Alliance for Human Rights. We look forward to its contribution to stronger partnerships, broader engagement, and more effective human rights action across regions and generations. Madam Chair, let me close this statement by zooming in on the reality of human rights lived today. Around the world, in this very moment, civil society organizations and human rights defenders working tirelessly to promote human rights are themselves subjected to intimidation, repression and violence. LGBTIQ persons continue to face discrimination, violence and hate. Restrictions on sexual and reproductive health and rights deny people autonomy over their own bodies and future. Children caught in conflict are deprived of education, protection and opportunities. And many, many more are unable to raise their voices. in this very moment and this very week to come. We owe it to them to take these negotiations seriously, to find common ground, to protect the systems and procedures in place, to safeguard the norms and strengthen human rights protection, because by doing so, we ultimately agree to create a safer world for all of us. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Sweden. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Panama.

Thank you, Madam Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegations, ladies and gentlemen. Allow me, Chair, to first begin by congratulating you and members of the Bureau for your election to chair over the work of our Third Committee. You can count on Panama's collaboration and commitment, Madam Chair. Discussions in this forum focus on numbers, indicators, resolutions, and other aspects that can be quantified. These are indispensable tools for our work. However, we must recall that behind each number there is a person, there is a mother, hoping that her daughter will be able to grow up without fear. There is a young person seeking opportunities to study and work. There is an older adult that aspires to live out this stage of his or her life with dignity. There is a child that should be learning and playing, not fleeing from violence. And this is why we are here. We are here for them. And this is why our work carries so much value. For our country, social development and human rights cannot be solely understood as abstract commitments. They should be translated into something much more tangible, into the possibility of a person living with dignity and a person being able to build his or her own future. And in 2026, this responsibility acquires particular urgency. we are increasingly closer to 2030. We have shown that the Sustainable Development Goals can deliver results. Nevertheless, progress in the process continues to be slow, insufficient and unequal. This should lead us to simply reflect. We already know a lot about what works. Now, what we need is the will to do this more swiftly and with cooperation and solidarity. In Panama, we consider that investing in people is one of the most important investments that a state can make. And this is why we continue strengthening our policies when it comes to education, health, social protection, and inclusion. We also continue to work in order to close gaps that affect populations that are most vulnerable. This includes our indigenous peoples and people of African descent, people living with disabilities, older adults, migrants, women, youth, boys, and girls. Madam Chair, I would like to specifically touch upon the issue of women and girls. The violence that millions of them continue to experience cannot merely become a number that we react indifferently to. When a woman lives with fear inside her own home, when a girl faces barriers to go to school, when an indigenous woman cannot fully participate in the decisions of her community, we are not just facing an individual problem, but rather a society that has still not fully realized its promise of equality. Panama continues to make progress through its Public Policy on Equal Opportunities for Women 2024-2034, by folding in gender in our policies for climate action and initiatives to strengthen the leadership of indigenous women. And we are firm in our commitment to the Beijing Platform of Action, but we know that policies and instruments really acquire value when a woman can feel results in her daily life. The same thing happens with our boys, girls, and adolescents. Protecting them is a legal and moral obligation, but it is so much more than that. It means deciding what kind of a society do we want to build. No child should grow up thinking that violence is something that is normal. No child should have to leave school because poverty and hunger decided for him or her. No child should become a victim of human trafficking, exploitation, or recruitment in a conflict that they never chose. This is why Panama will continue to champion comprehensive protection for children, and we will support international efforts to prevent grave violations against children. Madam Chair, we should also speak about trust. Corruption, transnational organized crime, and institutional weakness have consequences that are deeply human. When resources for a school, a hospital, or a social program do not reach those who need them, human rights are also affected. This is why Panama reaffirms its commitment to international cooperation in the areas of crime prevention, criminal justice, and the fight against corruption. We specifically value the presence in Panama of the UN Regional Office of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime for Central America and the Caribbean. We also value the joint work of the United Nations Program for Development, along with national institutions and other agencies, funds, and programs of the United Nations that, from their offices in Panama, contribute to sustainable development in the region. And in that very same spirit, Panama supports efforts to make the United Nations more efficient and effective. Efficiency, however, cannot be an end in and of itself. Each reform, each resource that we optimize, each duplication that we avoid should, at the end of the day, respond to a single question. Are we really reaching the people that need this organization, Madam Chair? We are living in a moment that is very complicated for multilateralism. Conflicts are multiplying, inequalities persist, and climate change hits the hardest those that have the least. And trust in our institutions is being stress tested. Given this scenario, we could sink into pessimism, but Panama, however, is choosing another path. We choose to believe in cooperation. We choose to believe that differences between states should not prevent us from recognizing what we share, what we have in common. And we choose to recall that human rights do not belong to a single country or region, culture or ideology. They belong to each person. As an elected member of the Security Council for 2025-2026, Panama has endeavored to take that conviction to this body by championing international peace and security and the protection of those that are in the greatest situations of vulnerability. Madam Chair, Agenda 2030 reminds us that no one should be left behind, but in recent years, Perhaps we should ask ourselves an even more challenging question. When we reach the end of this decade and we look back, will we be able to say that we did everything in our power so that the dignity that we champion in this room became a reality in people's lives? Panama. wants to be able to answer yes. And we will work alongside all of you to make it happen. I thank you.
